messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]          Admission Date: [REDACTED]      Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

History of Present Illness:
A 79-year-old male with a history of prostate cancer presented with progressively worsening double vision and eventual right eye ptosis. Neurological examination revealed complete third and sixth nerve palsies on the right side. MR imaging showed an enhancing soft tissue mass involving the clivus, pituitary fossa, cavernous sinus, and posterior nasal cavity. An endonasal transsphenoidal approach to the sphenoid sinus was carried out to obtain a biopsy of the lesion. A histopathological diagnosis of metastatic melanoma was made, and evaluation was undertaken by the oncology team.

Hospital Course Summary:
During the patient's hospital stay, he underwent a number of diagnostic tests and a biopsy following which he was diagnosed with metastatic melanoma. The medical team consulted with the oncology team, who evaluated the patient and recommended further treatment options. The patient's clinical condition stabilised, and he was discharged with the oncology team's recommended course of treatment.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's medical condition at discharge was stable, with no further significant neurological or ophthalmological deficits.

Discharge Medications:
No medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Follow-up Care:
The oncology team recommended further outpatient treatment and follow-up evaluations for the patient, which the patient accepted.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to follow up with the oncology team on a regular basis, and to report any new or concerning symptoms.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Discharge Condition:
Stable.

Discharge Plan:
The patient was discharged with the recommended course of treatment and follow-up evaluations by the oncology team.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The admission was for a skull-base mass (clivus, pituitary fossa, cavernous sinus) causing right third and sixth nerve palsies, which biopsy showed to be metastatic melanoma. Because the episode was for the secondary deposit, this belongs in chapter C under secondary malignant neoplasms. The clivus is bone, so the category is C79 (C79.5), though the code could shift if the coder treats the cavernous sinus or pituitary extension as the main site.

CODE: C79
